newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian communists see centre-left government soon.
newsitem.headline: Indian communists see centre-left government soon.

text.p: India's two main communist parties, heading an influential left-wing bloc in the ousted United Front coalition, said on Tuesday they were confident a new government would be formed by next week.
"A new government will be formed soon," a senior leader of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) told Reuters.
Asked if the government would be in place before a special budget session of parliament begins on April 21, he said: "It could be one or two days beyond that."
An official of the Communist Party of India (CPI) said the Left Front bloc, which is dominated by the two communist parties, would discuss its strategy at a meeting on Wednesday.
"We are of course clear that a new government has to be put in place to fight the threat to secularism," the official said.

Both parties said they would join a meeting of the United Front's decision-making Steering Committe on Thursday when a new leader is expected to be named to succeed caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
A United Front official said CPI-M general secretary Harkishan Singh Surjeet would brief the alliance later on Wednesday about the Left Front's decisions on a new government.
The new leader was to be formally endorsed by a meeting of the United Front's deputies scheduled for Sunday, a day before parliament meets to discuss the budget, the CPI official said.
The CPI-M is regarded as the author of Deve Gowda's centre-left alliance, which took power in June with the support of the Congress party following inconclusive elections.
India's main communist party, the CPI-M heads the influential Left Front, which controls 52 seats in the lower house of the hung parliament.

Congress withdrew support for the government on March 30 over its alleged failure to check the rise of the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), forcing Deve Gowda's defeat on Friday in a vote of confidence in parliament.
Despite their aversion to each other, the CPI-M and the BJP were united in their opposition to holding the planned budget session without a new government in place.

"It would not be fair either to parliament, or to democracy, or to the people of India if the special session became just another device to complete the economic agenda of a defeated government," the BJP told President Shankar Dayal Sharma in a letter.
CPI-M politburo member Sitaram Yechury echoed that view.
"Only in case Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament) is to be dissolved would there be a need to pass the finance bill," Yechury told the Press Trust of India.
"At this juncture, there are chances of a government being formed. So where is the need for hurry?" he said.
On Monday, Congress dropped its own bid for power and agreed to back the United Front under a new leader.
But Congress leader Pranab Mukherjee could not say how long his party would extend its support. "It will depend on their performance," he said.
The BJP is confident it would emerge strengthened from snap elections to the 542-member Lok Sabha, where it controls 193 votes with allies. The Congress has 140 members and the United Front 178.
